newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Soviet "mole" was betrayed by accident - book.
newsitem.headline: French Soviet "mole" was betrayed by accident - book.

text.p: A Soviet double-agent codenamed "Farewell" by his French handlers, who was one of the West's most-prized Moscow "moles", was inadvertently betrayed to his masters by a top French diplomat, a book due out next week says.

"Bonjour Farewell" by bilingual Russian historian Sergei Kostin contends that senior intelligence officer Vladimir Ippolitovitch Vetrov was accidentally betrayed to his KGB superiors during the shock expulsion from France of 47 Soviet "diplomats" in 1983.
He was arrested and executed after a secret trial in 1985.

Cold War historians say Vetrov was one of the West's most valuable assets ever in Moscow and supplied suitcase-loads of documents in the early 1980s which showed how deeply Western defences were penetrated by Moscow.
More importantly, according to Kostin's book, he pinpointed Western intelligence officers working for the Soviet Union.

Then president Francois Mitterrand impressed U.S. president Ronald Reagan at his first Western summit in Ottawa in 1981 by revealing the existence of "Farewell" to convince him France's new Socialist-led government could be trusted.
Vetrov's revelations led to a series of expulsions of Soviet diplomats from Western capitals on suspicion of spying but also ultimately to the agent's own doom, the book says.

It says Francois Scheer, now French ambassador to Germany and then chief of staff to foreign minister Claude Cheysson, inadvertedly led the KGB to "Farewell" when he notified the Soviet charge d'affaires in Paris that 47 of his subordinates were being expelled.
Expecting the envoy, Nikolai Afanassievsky, to deny the charges, Scheer showed him a top-secret Soviet document, passed on by Vetrov, which supported the espionage charges.
Afanassievsky's subsequent report to Moscow narrowed down the number of people who could have had access to the document to several dozen top intelligence officers, Kostin writes.
Vetrov confessed under interrogation and was shot after a trial behind closed doors.
The French embassy in Bonn declined comment but the daily Le Figaro quoted Scheer as saying he had had no idea of Vetrov's existence when he showed the document to the Soviet envoy.
At that time, "Farewell" was no longer at KGB headquarters supplying the West with information but in a Russian gulag prison camp serving a 15-year-sentence for murder.

An impulsive man frustrated by his failure to obtain an expected promotion in the KGB, he had a complicated private life and had tried to murder his mistress before killing a retired policeman who witnessed the scene, the book says.

Kostin criticises Vetrov's French handlers in Moscow, saying one was a crew-cut French military attache who looked so stereotyped that the KGB believed he was a decoy meant to shake them off the real trail.

The book says that when "Farewell" decided to work for the West, he chose to turn over his secrets to a French counter-espionage unit, knowing the KGB had such low regard for it that they hardly ever tried to track down its sources.
